name: Biscuit
lede: Biscuit is the pale tan of a baked biscuit, named from a word that means "twice cooked" and first used as a color in the 1880s.

sections.title: Twice-cooked
sections.body:
*Biscuit* comes from the Italian *biscotto*, "twice-cooked" [1]. As a color word it means the light brown of a biscuit, and the dictionary dates its first record as a color to 1884 [1].

The word has a second life in pottery: a clay body that has had its first firing but not yet been decorated is called biscuit [1].

sections.title: Biscuit in the wardrobe
sections.body: In fashion, biscuit sits among the soft skin-toned neutrals. A history of the color nude lists sand, champagne, biscuit, peach and beige as the alternatives that persist next to the word nude itself [2]. Its neighbors on the swatch chart are [[beige]], [[tan]] and [[bisque]] [3].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files this color under "brownish pink", in block 57, about 2.7 units of color difference from the swatch [3]. Ridgway's 1912 atlas and the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 are also sources for the name [3]. The color is light, with a lightness near 74 out of 100, and low in saturation [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The ColorHub archive places biscuit in the orange family, though its chroma is low: it is a muted, light brownish pink [3]. Contrast against white is about 2 to 1, which is too pale for body text [3].

origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, p. 50
